prompt: Explain how U.S. health insurance works using only fantasy football metaphors.
response:
Welcome to the most complicated, high-stakes league in the world: the U.S. Health Insurance system. It’s a mandatory keeper league where an injury to your top running back could bankrupt your entire franchise if you don’t understand the rules. 

Here is everything you need to know about navigating the rulebook:

**Open Enrollment (Draft Season)**
You only get one window a year to join the league or change your league format. If you miss Draft Day, you are locked out of the waiver wire for the whole year. The only exception is if you experience a "Qualifying Life Event"—like getting married (joining a co-manager) or having a baby (adding a rookie to your taxi squad). 

**Employer-Sponsored Plans (The Corporate League)**
Most managers get into the game through their job. Think of this as a company league where the CEO pays for 75% of your entry fee, and the rest is automatically deducted from your paycheck before you even see it. 

**Premiums (The Monthly League Buy-In)**
This is your entry fee, but instead of paying once in August, you pay it every single month. You have to pay this buy-in just to keep your team active, even if none of your players ever get hurt and you never look at the app. 

**In-Network vs. Out-of-Network (ESPN vs. Rogue Platforms)**
The League Commissioner has a strict list of approved players and managers (In-Network). If you trade within this approved ESPN/Yahoo ecosystem, your costs are predictable and capped. But if you try to pick up an "Out-of-Network" player—say, reaching into the CFL or a rogue independent league—the Commissioner will punish you. They won’t recognize the points, they won’t cover the transaction costs, and you’ll lose your shirt in penalty fees.

**Copay (The Roster Move Fee)**
Every time you want to make a simple, routine move—like subbing a player into your starting lineup (going in for a check-up)—the Commissioner charges you a flat transaction fee. Usually, it’s about $20 or $30. 

**The Deductible (Your Minimum FAAB Spend)**
This is the darkest part of the league. Let's say a massive injury bug hits your roster and you need to make serious waiver wire claims to survive. Even though you pay your monthly buy-in, the Commissioner won't help you pay for *any* of those waiver claims right away. You must spend your own Free Agent Acquisition Budget (FAAB) entirely out of pocket until you hit a specific number—say, $2,000. Until you spend $2,000 of your own money on waivers, you are playing solo.

**Coinsurance (The FAAB Split)**
Hooray, you spent $2,000 and finally met your deductible! Does the Commissioner pay for everything now? No. Now you enter the "Coinsurance" phase. The Commissioner agrees to a split. For every waiver wire pickup you make for the rest of the season, you pay 20% of the FAAB cost, and the Commissioner pays 80%. 

**The Out-of-Pocket Maximum (The Uncapped Waiver Wire)**
If your team suffers so many catastrophic ACL tears that your 20% coin-flip payments eventually add up to a massive limit (let's say $8,000), you finally unlock the ultimate league achievement. You have hit your Out-of-Pocket Max. For the rest of the season, the Commissioner covers 100% of your waiver claims. You have infinite FAAB until the season ends and the league resets in January.

**HMO vs. PPO (League Trade Settings)**
*   **PPO Leagues:** You have complete roster flexibility. You can trade with anyone, anywhere, at any time, as long as they are in-network. 
*   **HMO Leagues:** You are assigned a designated League Manager (a Primary Care Physician). If you want to make a trade to upgrade your tight end (see a Specialist), you are physically not allowed to do it until your League Manager gives you an official "Referral" slip saying it's okay.

**Pre-Existing Conditions (The Old Keeper Rules)**
Years ago, if you tried to switch to a new fantasy league while holding an injured Christian McCaffrey, the new Commissioner could say, "We aren't covering any costs related to McCaffrey because he was hurt before you joined." Thanks to a massive commissioner rule change a while back (The ACA), leagues are no longer allowed to ban you or deny your claims just because you walked into the draft with an injured roster. Every player is eligible, no matter how banged up they are.
